SALEM — Oregon lawmakers who want to spend $9\.3 billion on schools over the next two years will have to find a big chunk of funding in the remaining days of the legislative session, after Gov\. Kate Brown used a line-item veto to cut their appropriation from a savings account created to serve as a buffer against economic downturns\.

With huge revenue windfalls predicted in the current and next biennium, plus $2\.6 billion from the latest round of federal COVID aid, finding the money won’t be difficult\.

Brown notified Democratic leaders in the House and Senate of her line-item veto Tuesday, June 15\. It was the governor’s second veto this session, after she vetoed a motorcycle lane splitting bill citing public safety concerns\.

The governor’s latest veto was not surprising\. In mid-May, Brown raised concerns about lawmakers’ plan in a fiery letter in which she also questioned why they were boosting unrestricted school funding by hundreds of millions of dollars without making changes to reduce the opportunity gap for students historically inequitably served by schools, including low-income children and students of color\.

In her letter, Brown said that taking $200 million from the education stability fund would likely violate the Oregon Constitution because the state is doing well financially\. She encouraged lawmakers to use other money to raise the state school fund for 2021-2023 from $9\.1 billion to $9\.3 billion\.

The reserve account lawmakers wanted to tap is known as the education stability fund, and the governor noted in her letter that “the Oregon Constitution sets forth the limited circumstances in which the Legislature can access the principal in the \(fund\) — namely when the state is experiencing an economic downturn or facing some other emergency affecting school budgets\.”

The Legislature already withdrew $400 million from the education fund during a special session last summer and as of mid-May the balance stood at $415 million, according to state economist Josh Lehner\. Lawmakers did not use the withdrawal to increase the current $9 billion state school fund but rather to backfill anticipated declines in revenue including from income taxes\.

Last summer, it was early in the pandemic and the latest state revenue forecast showed the state could face a $2\.7 billion budget shortfall\. Tax revenues turned out to be much stronger than predicted and the state is now on track to bring in $1 billion more than expected this biennium\.

Lawmakers based their planned withdrawal from the reserve account on an opinion from the legislator’s top lawyer, Dexter Johnson, that they only needed one of the state’s quarterly revenue forecasts to predict at least a 2% drop from the May 2019 forecast on which the current budget was built — it did not matter if more recent forecasts showed a huge rebound, Johnson wrote\.

Although the $200 million appropriation remained in the state school fund bill, Senate Bill 5514, lawmakers appear to have dropped their effort to actually withdraw money from the education savings account\. The transfer is outlined in another bill, Senate Bill 226, and it has been sitting in committee without any action since May\.

Republicans in the Legislature, who along with some Democrats have pushed for a $9\.6 billion state school fund, seized on Brown’s line-item veto Wednesday\.

“I’m surprised that the governor has decided to double down on a ‘cuts’ budget for K-12 students at a time when we need to do all we can to help our kids recover from a year defined by isolation and unprecedented learning loss,” House Republican Leader Christine Drazan of Canby said in an emailed statement\.

Drazan has said the state should approve a $9\.6 billion school fund, the level advocated by teachers unions and school district officials, to support a full return to in-person classes in the fall\. Oregon schools are receiving $1\.1 billion in the latest round of federal aid and also got federal COVID funds in 2020\.

Brown and legislative budget writers originally proposed a $9\.1 billion state school fund, slightly higher than the amount legislative analysts said was necessary to maintain current services and programs\. District and union officials questioned aspects of that analysis, saying it underestimated their costs\. At the same time, some of the districts that could face layoffs in 2021-2023 are set to receive a proportionally smaller state funding allocation because their student enrollment consistently declined\.

The governor’s deputy communications director, Charles Boyle, said Brown agrees with lawmakers who want to raise the state school fund to $9\.3 billion\.

“Conversations are ongoing about how school funding can be used equitably to benefit students disproportionately impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic and historic disparities,” Boyle wrote in an email\. “The governor remains committed to continuing to work closely with leaders of communities of color, legislators, and education leaders to take concrete steps to further equity in K-12 education this year\.”

Published 3:01 pm Wednesday, June 16, 2021

**By Hillary Borrud  
The Oregonian**

Oregon lawmakers who want to spend $9\.3 billion on schools over the next two years will have to find a big chunk of funding in the remaining days of the legislative session, after Gov\. Kate Brown used a line-item veto to cut their appropriation from a savings account created to serve as a buffer against economic downturns\.

With huge revenue windfalls predicted in the current and next biennium, plus $2\.6 billion from the latest round of federal COVID aid, finding the money won’t be difficult\.

Brown notified Democratic leaders in the House and Senate of her line-item veto Tuesday\. It was the governor’s second veto this session, after she vetoed a motorcycle lane splitting bill citing public safety concerns\.

The governor’s latest veto was not surprising\. In mid-May, Brown raised concerns about lawmakers’ plan in a fiery letter in which she also questioned why they were boosting unrestricted school funding by hundreds of millions of dollars without making changes to reduce the opportunity gap for students historically inequitably served by schools, including low-income children and students of color\.

In her letter Tuesday, Brown said that taking $200 million from the education stability fund would likely violate the Oregon Constitution because the state is doing well financially\. She encouraged lawmakers to use other money to raise the state school fund for 2021-2023 from $9\.1 billion to $9\.3 billion\.

The reserve account lawmakers wanted to tap is known as the education stability fund, and the governor noted in her letter that “the Oregon Constitution sets forth the limited circumstances in which the Legislature can access the principal in the \(fund\) — namely when the state is experiencing an economic downturn or facing some other emergency affecting school budgets\.”

The Legislature already withdrew $400 million from the education fund during a special session last summer and as of mid-May the balance stood at $415 million, according to state economist Josh Lehner\. Lawmakers did not use the withdrawal to increase the current $9 billion state school fund but rather to backfill anticipated declines in revenue including from income taxes\.

Last summer, it was early in the pandemic and the latest state revenue forecast showed the state could face a $2\.7 billion budget shortfall\. Tax revenues turned out to be much stronger than predicted and the state is now on track to bring in $1 billion more than expected this biennium\.

Lawmakers based their planned withdrawal from the reserve account on an opinion from the legislator’s top lawyer, Dexter Johnson, that they only needed one of the state’s quarterly revenue forecasts to predict at least a 2% drop from the May 2019 forecast on which the current budget was built — it did not matter if more recent forecasts showed a huge rebound, Johnson wrote\.

Although the $200 million appropriation remained in the state school fund bill, Senate Bill 5514, lawmakers appear to have dropped their effort to actually withdraw money from the education savings account\. The transfer is outlined in another bill, Senate Bill 226, and it has been sitting in committee without any action since May\.

Republicans in the Legislature, who along with some Democrats have pushed for a $9\.6 billion state school fund, seized on Brown’s line-item veto Wednesday\.

“I’m surprised that the governor has decided to double down on a ‘cuts’ budget for K-12 students at a time when we need to do all we can to help our kids recover from a year defined by isolation and unprecedented learning loss,” House Republican Leader Christine Drazan of Canby said in an emailed statement\.

Drazan has said the state should approve a $9\.6 billion school fund, the level advocated by teachers unions and school district officials, to support a full return to in-person classes in the fall\. Oregon schools are receiving $1\.1 billion in the latest round of federal aid and also got federal COVID funds in 2020\.

Brown and legislative budget writers originally proposed a $9\.1 billion state school fund, slightly higher than the amount legislative analysts said was necessary to maintain current services and programs\. District and union officials questioned aspects of that analysis, saying it underestimated their costs\. At the same time, some of the districts that could face layoffs in 2021-2023 are set to receive a proportionally smaller state funding allocation because their student enrollment consistently declined\.

The governor’s deputy communications director, Charles Boyle, said Brown agrees with lawmakers who want to raise the state school fund to $9\.3 billion\.

“Conversations are ongoing about how school funding can be used equitably to benefit students disproportionately impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic and historic disparities,” Boyle wrote in an email\. “The governor remains committed to continuing to work closely with leaders of communities of color, legislators, and education leaders to take concrete steps to further equity in K-12 education this year\.”

# Legislative education leaders push back on Moss Point School District's claim that teacher pay raises are causing shortfall

Moss Point High School \(Photo from Moss Point School District's Facebook page\)

- ***“Everything that they’re saying is untrue,” House Education Chairman Rob Roberson said Thursday\. “The teacher pay increase was funded by the State of Mississippi\.”***

The Moss Point School District claims to be facing a projected $2\.5 million deficit for Fiscal Year 2027\. District leaders are blaming the shortfall on the teacher pay raise signed into law this year\.

The district’s financial consultant Bonnie Granger told WLOX that the shortfall is largely tied to an unfunded state teacher pay raise\.

“Most of that was brought on by the teacher \[pay raise\] — even though the teachers very well deserve it — but the state didn’t fund any of the teacher pay raise for this district,” Granger said\.

State Rep\. Rob Roberson \(R\), the chairman of the House Education Committee, takes exception with that claim\.

“Everything that they’re saying is untrue,” Roberson told Magnolia Tribune Thursday morning\. “The teacher pay increase was funded by the State of Mississippi\.”

Roberson said the district is likely having shortfalls because of student population loss while not properly adjusting to the new realities that decline creates\.

“Anytime you start getting under 1,500 or 2,000 students, you’re going to have a larger problem, especially if your administration is top heavy,” Roberson explained\.

House Education Committee Chair Rob Roberson \(R\), addresses the House committee, February 2026 \(Photo by Jeremy Pittari \| Magnolia Tribune\)

According to the latest student population data from the Mississippi Department of Education, Moss Point School District reported 1,519 enrolled students from PreK to 12th Grade in the 2025-2026 school year, a drop of nearly 500 students over the last decade\. Fifty of those students were enrolled in PreK, a program which did not exist in the district in the 2015-2016 school year\. Moss Point High School reported less than 425 students\.

“In business, you have to make these hard decisions,” the House chairman added\. “These school districts have never had to think that way until now\.”

Roberson said he planned to ask the Mississippi Department of Education to review where “their money is going\.”

State Senator Dennis DeBar \(R\), the chairman of the Senate Education Committee, shared a similar sentiment\.

“We funded the teacher pay raise and we allocated the money based on the number of students under the formula,” DeBar told Magnolia Tribune\. “The amount of money that we appropriated for the teacher pay raise was based on the number of teachers\. However, the funding for that went inside the \[student funding\] formula this year\. And so, what that means is that the funding is based on the number of students\. Some districts, like Moss Point, that don’t have the number of students of say a Rankin County maybe got less money \[from the formula\]\.”

Yet, DeBar added, “The money is there\. They knew about it, especially with the hold harmless going away\.”

Senate Education Committee Chair Dennis DeBar \(R\) met with his fellow committee members on Tuesday to start the 2026 legislative session off by taking up three bills\. \(Photo by Jeremy Pittari \| Magnolia Tribune\)

When lawmakers passed the new student funding formula in 2024, certain districts like Moss Point that were receiving more funding than what their student population would allow for under the new formula were given a three year hold harmless provision\. That provision meant funding for those school districts would not decrease from what was received in the 2023-2024 school year during that transition period\.

Lawmakers said at the time that the hold harmless provision was for the school districts’ planning purposes, allowing local school boards time to make cuts where needed before the provision expired in 2027\.

The Moss Point School District had proposed an ad valorem tax increase for the upcoming fiscal year but following local backlash school officials set that aside for now\.

In her interview with WLOX, Granger did add that the district is working with Jackson County and the City of Moss Point while exploring a possible exception “to the 55 mill cap that we could use for next year when we lose the hold-harmless provision\.”

Senator DeBar believes the district has had ample time to prepare for the changes\.

“They would have had to come up with the money this year or next year from their local budget but this year was a better year for \[the teacher pay raises\] because next year when you’re losing the hold harmless that would have been a double whammy,” DeBar said\.

State Rep\. Roberson was more pointed in his criticism of Moss Point School District’s claims\.

“They have been given plenty of time, even if they did not get held harmless,” Roberson said\. “My best guess is that they’re not capable of running their own school\.”

Community colleges in North Texas will likely be shortchanged by millions of dollars in state funding in the upcoming fiscal year, after those colleges overperformed on a student success incentive program that Texas can no longer afford to pay\.

Last week, the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board approved changes to a program that financially rewards community colleges for getting low-income students and adult students to graduation day\. Across the state, community colleges have exceeded expectations on those metrics, and the total amount due to the colleges is now millions of dollars more than the amount the board is allowed to distribute before the next legislative session\. The incentive program, which was outlined in House Bill 8,went into effect in 2023\.

Schools will now earn smaller bonuses for those student outcomes\. Officials with the THECB said the cutback will be “necessary to ensure the financial sustainability” of the community college financing program as a whole\.

State estimates show that Dallas College and Tarrant County College may be affected by the funding change\.

In fiscal year 2027, Dallas College is expected to get 2\.8% less funding than was promised, amounting to just over $3 million\. In the years since HB 8 passed, Dallas College’s funding has increased 15%, the projection shows\.

At Tarrant County College, close to 6\.5% of funding could be lost, which amounts to $4\.1 million\. Neither Dallas nor Tarrant colleges are expected to be the hardest hit across the state; nearly a dozen schools are expected to lose 15% of their funding, and Texarkana College administrators are bracing for a nearly 25% slash\.

Collin County College is one of only a handful of systems that may actually see their funding increase under the change\. State projections expect the school to get 7\.1%, or $4\.2 million, in additional funding next fiscal year\.

While the state legislature could vote to fund the gap in the upcoming session, it is unclear whether there will be support for the measure at a time when leading officials are urging spending cuts\. Spokespeople from Dallas College and Tarrant County College did not respond to the Observer’s request for comment\.

Colleges are now grappling with the funding change at the same time as Gov\. Greg Abbott has urged public colleges and universities not to raise tuition through the next academic year\. Still, some college leaders testified before a state Senate committee that the funding changes will inevitably result in job cuts,and will make it difficult to continue funding the same programs that contributed to the HB 8 student success boom\.

In Tarrant County, Tarrant County College District trustees have questioned how the school is expected to “sit here and let people arbitrarily decide to take money continuously away\.” Even as state funding drops, officials are not expecting the college to have a revenue decline, although the change to state funding could affect whether employee raises are given as planned, the Fort Worth Report reports\.

# Perth Protest Latest Live News: Students Rally Against Pauline Hanson and One Nation; Why Is the Protest Being Held? Key Demands Explained

**Perth Protest Latest Live News: **Thousands of high school and university students gathered at Forrest Place in Perth CBD on Thursday, August 13, as part of a nationwide student protest against One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and the party’s policies\. The Perth event was one of several demonstrations organised under the banner “Students Say No to Hanson\.”

The nationwide action was organised by the National Union of Students \(NUS\), with students in multiple Australian cities joining the walkouts\. Organisers said the protests were aimed at opposing what they described as One Nation’s racist and divisive political agenda\.

## Perth Protest Today: Why Are Students Protesting Pauline Hanson?

The students are protesting against the rise of One Nation and what organisers describe as the party’s racist, divisive and far-right policies\. Student organisers have also raised concerns about issues including education funding, workers’ rights, housing and the cost of living\. The NUS has specifically criticised Hanson’s record on education, including her opposition to measures such as free TAFE and increased funding for public schools\. The Perth protest was scheduled for 1pm to 3pm at Forrest Place, with the event forming part of the nationwide day of action\.

## Perth Student Protest: What Are Their Key Demands?

The protesters’ central message is opposition to Pauline Hanson and One Nation\. Their broader demands and concerns include:

- Opposition to racism and discrimination: Student organisers say they want to challenge political rhetoric they believe targets migrant and minority communities\.
- A more inclusive Australia: Protesters have called for a future that is not shaped by racist or divisive politics\.
- Better education support: Student groups have raised concerns about public education funding and policies affecting schools and tertiary education\.
- Action on cost-of-living pressures: Economic pressures affecting young people and their families have also featured in the wider student campaign\.
- Youth participation in politics: Organisers argue that students should have a voice on political issues that will affect their future\.

The protest is therefore not simply focused on a single policy\. It represents a broader student campaign against One Nation’s political direction and its growing electoral support\.

## Perth Protest Latest Live News: What Did Students Say?

At the Perth demonstration, students criticised the idea that young people should remain politically silent until they reach voting age\. A Perth Hills high school student named Sadie, who was among the speakers at the event, said high school students were encouraged to stay silent, to stay to the back until they are 18, like voting once every three years is a privilege to look forward to\.

She also said, “We are meant to watch our schools lose funding, a genocide unfold, and the cost of living go up exponentially\. And you just want us to finish our maths homework\.” Sadie argued that students have historically played an important role in political protests and said young people would ultimately live with the consequences of decisions made today\.

She also rejected claims that students were simply skipping school or had been influenced by teachers\. “We are not fighting on behalf of an organisation or as a means to skip school\. We are not stupid kids wanting to sit at the adult table\. We believe in getting Hanson’s fascist ideas out of our country,” she said\.

## Perth Protest Latest Live News: How Did Pauline Hanson Respond?

Pauline Hanson criticised the student walkouts and said schools should focus on teaching students how to form their own views\. In a post on social media, Hanson said schools should “teach young Australians how to think, not what to think”\.

She also urged young people to focus their attention on economic pressures, writing, “If you want to protest something, protest why your parents’ wages are going backwards and the cost of everything is going up,”

Hanson added, “The Labor Greens government is selling out your future, and you’ll inherit a weaker, poorer and less safe country\. Whether you know it or not, One Nation and I are fighting for you\.”

## Perth Protest Latest Live News: Politicians Question Student Participation

The protests have also triggered criticism from One Nation figures and other politicians\. One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce accused “socialist” and “left-wing” teachers of encouraging students to join demonstrations against the party\. He argued that students should be in school rather than participating in political protests\.

Federal Education Minister Jason Clare also encouraged students to remain in class and suggested that those wishing to demonstrate could do so outside school hours\.

The debate has consequently expanded beyond One Nation’s policies to questions about student political participation, school attendance and the role of teachers in political education\.

## Perth Protest Latest Live News: What Happens Next?

The Perth demonstration is part of a coordinated national campaign involving students in cities including Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide, Canberra, Wollongong and Newcastle\.

Student organisers say they intend to continue speaking out against what they regard as racist and divisive politics, while Hanson and her supporters have defended One Nation’s policies and questioned the political influence behind the protests\.

For Perth, the key issue remains the growing political engagement of young Australians and their opposition to One Nation as the party gains greater attention in national politics\.

# YouTubers enter Saurav Das' residence in Delhi, complaint filed

YouTube mediapersons enters Saurav Das' house in Delhi

**New Delhi:** Cockroach Janta Party \(CJP\) chief spokesperson Saurav Das on Wednesday, August 5, alleged that a group of YouTubers and mediapersons entered his residence and filmed its interiors, prompting him to appeal to the Delhi Police, and said the incident poses a serious security threat to his family\.

Das, who said he was in Maharashtra attending the two-day meeting of the Cockroach Janta Party, alleged in posts on X that 15-20 people reached his residence on Wednesday morning, while some had been stationed outside since the previous night\.

Independent digital media platform The Pamphlet shared a video on its social media handles from outside Das’ residence in Delhi’s GK-1 residential neighbourhood\. The reporter questioned how Das could afford a high-rent house in an upscale locality as a student\.

“The question remains, where did an ordinary student get so much money? He comes from a middle-class family and does not have significant financial support from his parents\. Questions are being raised about the source of funding for the CJP protests,” the reporter is heard saying\.

They moved past the gate and peeked through the window of the house, noting that the house appears empty\.

“Certain YouTubers and media channels have broken into my house and are showing the visuals from inside\. It’s not just an invasion of my privacy but also a grave security threat for me and my family,” he said\.

Warning of possible consequences, Das said, “If anti-social elements attack me at my residence as a result of this, these YouTubers and their troll handlers who are coordinating this will be directly responsible\.

In a subsequent post, he claimed that the videos had “activated goons” and created a “grave security threat for everyone living in the house\.”

# Singapore start-up Ropedia raises US$22 mil in pre-Series A round for robot-training data

The robotics data company has raised US$30 million so far, and will use the latest funds to gather more training data, increase device production and expand in Singapore and the US\.

Ropedia, a Singapore start-up that supplies training data for robots and physical artificial intelligence systems, has raised US$22 million \($28\.4 million\) in a pre-Series A funding round\.

It did not identify the investors in the latest round, saying only that it was led by venture firms with experience in AI, deep technology and infrastructure in Southeast Asia\.

The deal brings its total funding to US$30 million\. An earlier round included investors and individuals connected to Google, Andreessen Horowitz, Nvidia and Amazon, according to the company\.

Ropedia's proprietary wearable devices record first-person video, depth, movement and audio as people carry out physical tasks\. The company processes that information into training material for developers seeking to teach robots how to perform tasks in real-world settings\. It offers the data through its Xperience-10M product and customised services\.

\"A robot can't play baseball by watching a video any more than you could learn to ride a bike by reading about it\. The robot must understand what it's like to grip a bat and know the timing it takes to hit a ball\. That's the information Ropedia's technology provides, and it's why this investment matters,\" says Zhaoxi Chen, CEO and co-founder of Ropedia\.

He continues: \"Our technology lets robots capture the experience and real judgment it will take for them to move through the world\. If we get all that right, the robots will leave the beta stage and start doing real work, first in factories, then at home, with families\.\"

According to Ropedia, its approach can reduce data-collection costs by as much as 50 times compared with traditional methods\.

Its wearable device has entered mass production, and the company is already working with more than 20 robotics and foundation-model companies in North America, China and Singapore\.

Ropedia will use the fresh funds to expand data collection in Southeast Asia and North America, increase production of its wearable devices and grow its teams in Singapore and the US\.

It also plans to add tools for annotating and checking data, strengthen its compliance systems and expand research into data foundation models and world models\.

Ropedia was founded in the second half of 2025 by Chen, chief technology officer Fangzhou Hong and chief scientist Ziwei Liu, an associate professor at Nanyang Technological University\.
